intro:
This track is about what happens when many people change the same data at once, or when a change has to land on two machines. A transaction is a group of changes that a database treats as one: all of them happen, or none do. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows: two payments from one account in the same second, a meeting room booked twice, a month-end report that adds up balances while people keep paying, and a coffee paid from an app wallet that never reaches the café. Then they open up what the database does about each one.

By the end, you can:

- say what a transaction promises, what the four promises called ACID really buy, and why "ACID compliant" says little about what you get by default;
- draw each race between two transactions as a timeline (a lost update, write skew, a phantom) and predict what PostgreSQL's Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable levels do about it, and what Oracle and MySQL do under the same names;
- stop each race with the cheapest fix that works: a subtraction inside the UPDATE, a row lock, `SKIP LOCKED`, a constraint, or Serializable with a retry loop that can't charge a customer twice;
- explain the four ways databases keep transactions apart (old versions of rows, locks held until commit, a check that watches reads and writes, and one thread running one transaction at a time) and what each one costs;
- commit one change on two machines with two-phase commit, say what a crashed coordinator does to everyone's locks, and tell when a saga is the better design;
- say how far a transaction reaches in DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cassandra, and when a better layout of the data needs no transaction at all.

The eight lessons:

1. What a transaction promises: ACID and isolation levels
2. Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues
3. Write skew and phantoms: when there is no row to lock
4. MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM
5. Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI
6. Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua
7. Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA
8. Transactions in NoSQL

You need to read a little code, in Kotlin or Java, and to have Docker on your laptop. Docker is a free program that runs small, separate machines, called containers, on your own computer. You don't need any database background: every term is explained the first time it appears in a lesson. Earlier tracks help, and lessons name them when they lean on them: the write-ahead log from Storage engines, Redis from Caching, and copies and slices of data from Replication and Partitioning.

The labs are Kotlin with JUnit tests, one package per lesson (`sfz.txn.l01` to `sfz.txn.l08`), in whichever lab module has the tools the lesson needs. Lessons 1 to 3 and 7 use the `sql` module: their tests start PostgreSQL 18 in a container and run real sessions side by side. Lessons 4 and 5 build a store that keeps old versions of rows and a lock manager in plain Kotlin, in the `internals` module, with no Docker. Lesson 6 runs Redis 8.10 in the `redis` module and shows every sample in both Java and Kotlin. Lesson 8 builds Paxos in Kotlin and a MongoDB 9.0 transfer, in the `nosql` module. Run `./gradlew :<module>:test --tests 'sfz.txn.lNN.*'` from `labs/` until it passes. The Try its run in each database's own shell (psql, redis-cli, mongosh, cqlsh) against the services in `labs/env/`: `postgres.yml`, `redis.yml`, `mongo.yml`, `cassandra.yml`, and `cassandra6.yml` for the optional Accord step.
cheatsheet:
## The picture

A transaction's changes take effect at one moment, when its commit record reaches the write-ahead log (the database's notebook on disk), or not at all. Isolation decides what other transactions running at the same time see before and after that moment. Serializable means the result is the same as running the transactions one at a time, in some order. Across machines there is no single commit record, so every participant promises first, and one durable decision commits them all.

## The races, and PostgreSQL's levels (lessons 1 to 3)

| Race | What happens | Read Committed | Repeatable Read (snapshot isolation) | Serializable (SSI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dirty read | you read a change that is later undone | never | never | never |
| read skew | two reads in one transaction disagree | allowed | prevented | prevented |
| lost update | two read, change, write cycles; one write erases the other | allowed, silently | 40001 for the second writer | 40001 |
| write skew | both check a rule, then each changes a different row | allowed | allowed | 40001 |
| phantom | both check that a row doesn't exist, then both insert one | allowed | allowed | 40001 |

Names differ between databases. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server start at Read Committed. Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, so write skew gets through. MySQL's default REPEATABLE READ loses updates without an error, and its SERIALIZABLE uses two-phase locking. Hermitage, a public table of tests, shows what each level does in each database.

## Fixes, cheapest first (lessons 2 and 3)

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| lost update | subtract inside the UPDATE: `SET x = x - n`; or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, then work out the new value; or `UPDATE ... WHERE version = :v` and try again on 0 rows; or Repeatable Read with a retry |
| a to-do list of jobs shared by workers | `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1`; `NOWAIT` fails at once with 55P03 |
| write skew over rows that exist | `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` the rows the rule reads |
| phantom (a rule about a row that isn't there yet) | lock a parent row, or a slot row; `UNIQUE`; `EXCLUDE USING gist`; `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` (PostgreSQL 18); or Serializable |
| deadlock | lock rows in a fixed order (by ascending id); cap waits with `lock_timeout` |

## Old versions of rows: MVCC (lesson 4)

- An UPDATE in PostgreSQL writes a whole new version of the row and stamps the old one with its own transaction id as the deleter (`t_xmax`). Readers don't wait for writers, and writers don't wait for readers. Writers of the same row still wait for each other.
- A snapshot says which transactions a reader can see. A version is visible if the snapshot sees its creator, and its deleter is 0 or not seen. Read Committed takes a new snapshot for every statement, Repeatable Read one for the whole transaction.
- VACUUM removes versions whose deleter committed before the horizon, the oldest snapshot still in use. One long-open or prepared transaction holds it back for the whole database. Autovacuum freezes old versions at 200 million transaction ids of age.
- PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the table itself. MySQL's InnoDB and Oracle rebuild them from an undo log.

## Four ways to keep transactions apart (lessons 4 to 6)

| Approach | How | What it costs | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| snapshot isolation | old versions plus a snapshot per transaction; the first writer of a row wins | write skew gets through | PostgreSQL Repeatable Read, Oracle SERIALIZABLE, MongoDB |
| strict two-phase locking | shared and exclusive locks, all held until commit | readers block writers; deadlocks; 208 requests a second on the RUBiS test | MySQL SERIALIZABLE, SQL Server |
| SSI | a snapshot plus SIREAD notes that block nobody; abort a transaction caught in a dangerous pattern | false alarms and retries; 422 requests a second on RUBiS, against 435 for snapshot isolation | PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE |
| serial execution | one thread per partition runs each transaction to the end; transactions arrive whole, as stored procedures | one core per partition; one slow transaction stalls everyone; about 1,000 cross-partition writes a second in VoltDB | Redis, VoltDB |

## Error codes and what your code does

| Code | Meaning | What your code does |
|---|---|---|
| 40001 | serialization failure | run the whole transaction again, reads included |
| 40P01 | deadlock detected (after `deadlock_timeout`, 1 s) | run the whole transaction again |
| 55P03 | lock not available (`NOWAIT`, `lock_timeout`) | wait a little and try later; don't hold the line |
| 23505 | unique violation | an answer, not a glitch: don't retry |
| MongoDB `TransientTransactionError` | write conflict, or another passing failure | cancel and run the whole transaction again |
| DynamoDB `TransactionConflict` | another transaction was in flight on an item | retry after a short random wait, with the same client token |

## Redis (lesson 6)

Each command runs alone on Redis's single thread. `MULTI`/`EXEC` runs a batch with nothing in between, and never rolls back. `WATCH` makes `EXEC` return nil if a watched key changed, so a check made in your code becomes check-and-set. `EVALSHA` runs a cached Lua script, which reads, decides and writes in one step; reload it on `NOSCRIPT`. `FUNCTION LOAD` keeps functions with the data. A pipeline saves round trips but isn't atomic. Redis Cluster refuses keys from different slots with `CROSSSLOT`.

## One change on two machines (lesson 7)

1. Prepare: each participant saves its work to disk, keeps its locks and votes yes or no. `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'txf-1@wallets'`.
2. Decide: the coordinator writes `txf-1 COMMIT` to its log on disk. That line is the commit point. No line means abort (presumed abort).
3. Commit: `COMMIT PREPARED 'gid'` on each participant, retried until it answers, from a session in the same database.

`max_prepared_transactions` is 0 by default and needs a restart. `pg_prepared_xacts` lists in-doubt work; its locks show with no process id, and `pg_blocking_pids` reports them as 0. In-doubt transactions survive restarts, block writers and hold back VACUUM. XA (JTA in Java) puts the coordinator and its log inside your program. Three-phase commit needs delays with an upper limit, which real networks don't have. Percolator keeps the commit point in a primary lock next to the data. A saga commits each step locally and undoes with compensations, with no isolation between steps.

## NoSQL transactions (lesson 8)

| Store | How far one transaction reaches | When two writers collide |
|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | `TransactWriteItems`: up to 100 items, 4 MB, one Region; two writes per item | `TransactionCanceledException` with `TransactionConflict`; retry with the same client token (good for 10 minutes) |
| MongoDB 9.0 | many documents, on a replica set or sharded cluster; 60 s by default; at most 10,000 open | `WriteConflict` labelled `TransientTransactionError`: run the whole transaction again |
| Cassandra 5.0 | a lightweight transaction on one partition, Paxos, 4 round trips | `[applied] = False` and the current row |
| Cassandra 6.0 (alpha) | Accord: `BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT TRANSACTION` across partitions | put in order before it runs |

## Pairs people mix up

| | | The difference |
|---|---|---|
| Two-phase locking | Two-phase commit | Locking: hold every lock until commit, so transactions on one database stay apart. Commit: prepare everywhere, then decide once, so one transaction lands on several machines. |
| Lost update | Write skew | Lost update: two writers of the same row, and one write erases the other. Write skew: each writes a different row, and the rule they both checked breaks. |
| Write skew | Phantom | Write skew: the rule reads rows that exist, so you can lock them. Phantom: the rule looks for a row that isn't there yet, so there is nothing to lock. |
| Snapshot isolation | Serializable | Snapshot: each transaction reads one moment, and only two writers of one row clash. Serializable: the result matches some one-at-a-time order, so write skew is caught too. |
| Deadlock | In doubt | Deadlock: two transactions wait for each other, and the database aborts one. In doubt: a participant waits for a coordinator that may never come back, and nothing aborts it. |
| Rollback | Compensation | Rollback: the change never becomes visible. Compensation: a new step, such as a refund, that undoes a change people may already have seen. |

## Retries

Run the whole transaction again on 40001, 40P01, `TransientTransactionError`, `TransactionConflict` and lost connections, a few times, with waits that grow and have some randomness. A COMMIT whose answer was lost may have committed, so a retry is safe only with an idempotency key, a unique id per payment under a UNIQUE constraint.
recap: A transaction groups changes so they happen together or not at all, at one moment: when its commit record reaches the log. ACID's I, isolation, is the hard part, and "ACID compliant" says little about which level you get by default.

Every race is a timeline of two transactions. A lost update is two read, change, write cycles on one row. Write skew is two checks of one rule, then writes to different rows. A phantom is two checks that a row doesn't exist, then two inserts. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read stops lost updates but not write skew; Serializable stops all three, at the price of retries.

Fix it in the data first: subtract inside the UPDATE, `FOR UPDATE` on the rows a rule reads, `SKIP LOCKED` for a shared to-do list of jobs, and constraints (UNIQUE, EXCLUDE, WITHOUT OVERLAPS) for rules about rows that don't exist yet.
MVCC keeps old versions of rows so readers never wait for writers; writers of one row still take turns. One long-open or prepared transaction holds VACUUM's cleanup back for the whole database.

Four ways to keep transactions apart: snapshots (write skew gets through), strict two-phase locking (blocking and deadlocks), SSI (reads never wait, a few retries, a few percent slower than snapshots in its authors' tests), and serial execution (one thread, transactions arriving whole, slices of data).

A deadlock is a cycle of waits: the database finds it and aborts one transaction, and locking in a fixed order prevents it. Every transaction needs a retry loop, and a COMMIT whose answer was lost needs an idempotency key.

Across machines, two-phase commit: every participant promises, one durable record decides, then all commit. A dead coordinator leaves participants in doubt holding their locks, and XA puts that coordinator inside your own program.

NoSQL transactions exist, with limits and prices: DynamoDB's two-phase commit backed by a copied ledger, MongoDB's snapshot transactions, Cassandra's one-partition Paxos and its alpha Accord. Often one document, one conditional write or a saga is the better design.

quiz.q: A transfer's COMMIT was sent, and the connection dropped before the answer came back. The program runs the whole transfer again. What makes that retry safe?
options: Nothing extra: a transaction that didn't confirm was rolled back
Running the retry at SERIALIZABLE
An idempotency key stored under a UNIQUE constraint in the same transaction, because the first COMMIT may have succeeded
Waiting `deadlock_timeout` before the retry
quiz.why: The commit may have reached the log before the connection died, so the retry could apply the transfer twice. A unique idempotency key makes the second attempt fail with 23505, which the program reads as "already done". Assuming an unconfirmed commit rolled back is the tempting mistake. Isolation levels and deadlock settings do nothing about a lost answer.

quiz.q: Ten workers each run `SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE`, then mark the job running and commit. Ten workers get through jobs no faster than one. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Every worker picks the same first row and waits for the worker holding it; `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets each take the next job nobody holds
FOR UPDATE locks the whole table; use FOR SHARE
The pool has too few connections; raise it to ten
The query needs SERIALIZABLE to let workers run in parallel
quiz.why: All ten see the same oldest job and queue on its row lock, so they run one at a time. SKIP LOCKED steps over rows other transactions hold. FOR UPDATE locks rows, not the table, and FOR SHARE would let two workers take the same job. More connections or a stricter level don't remove the queue.

quiz.q: A booking app checks for clashes with `SELECT booking_id FROM bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && :slot FOR UPDATE`, finds none, and inserts, all under Repeatable Read. Two overlapping bookings for room 4 arrive at once. What happens?
options: The second one waits on the first one's FOR UPDATE lock, then sees the booking and refuses
Both commit: the check found no rows, so FOR UPDATE locked nothing, and the two inserts don't clash
The second insert fails with 40001, because Repeatable Read notices the clash
Both fail with a deadlock
quiz.why: This is a phantom: the rule is about rows that don't exist yet, so there is nothing to lock. Repeatable Read only catches two writers of the same row, and these inserts write different rows. An exclusion constraint (`EXCLUDE USING gist`) or PostgreSQL 18's `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` makes the database refuse the second insert; SERIALIZABLE would also catch it, with 40001.

quiz.q: A Repeatable Read report transaction has been open for three hours while payments keep changing `accounts`. What happens to the table?
options: Nothing: the report holds no locks, so it costs nothing
The payments wait until the report commits
The report's snapshot starts seeing the new versions after an hour
VACUUM can't remove versions replaced after the report's snapshot, so dead versions pile up and the table grows
quiz.why: VACUUM can remove a version only once no running transaction might still need it, and the report keeps that horizon pinned at its start. Readers never block writers under MVCC, so the payments keep going, and a Repeatable Read snapshot never changes during the transaction. A prepared transaction left in doubt has the same effect.

quiz.q: Under PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE, a 20-second report reads `settlements` while 1,000 inserts into it commit. What do the report's SIREAD notes do to the inserts?
options: Nothing during the inserts: SIREAD notes never block. A dangerous pattern may still make one transaction fail with 40001 later
They make each insert wait until the report commits
They make each insert fail with 40001 at once
They turn into a lock on the whole table after 1,000 rows
quiz.why: SSI's SIREAD notes, which PostgreSQL calls SIREAD locks, only record what a transaction read. Writers never wait for them, and they can't cause a deadlock. The check for read-write patterns decides at write or commit time whether someone must abort. Waiting on read locks is what strict two-phase locking does: the tempting answer, from MySQL's SERIALIZABLE.

quiz.q: On Redis Cluster, a Lua script that moves money from `wallet:7:main` to `wallet:9:main` fails with `CROSSSLOT`. What does this say about serial execution in general?
options: Lua scripts can't write two keys
The cluster is set up wrongly and should allow scripts across slots

A serial engine runs each partition on its own thread; a transaction across partitions needs coordination, which Redis Cluster refuses and VoltDB runs at about 1,000 writes a second. Keep a transaction's keys in one partition (hash tags) or change the design
The script must be sent with EVALSHA instead of EVAL
quiz.why: Serial execution is fast because each partition's thread needs no locks. Crossing partitions brings coordination back, so VoltDB runs such transactions in lockstep at a small fraction of its normal rate, and Redis Cluster refuses them. Hash tags such as `{wallet:7}:main` and `{wallet:7}:hold` keep one customer's keys together; a transfer between two customers' wallets needs another design, such as a saga.

quiz.q: A coordinator prepared a payment on two PostgreSQL databases, wrote `txf-5 COMMIT` to its log, committed the first database, and crashed. What should happen to `txf-5@payouts`, still listed in `pg_prepared_xacts` and holding the café's row?
options: Roll it back, since its coordinator is gone and the row is blocking the café's payments
Leave it: PostgreSQL rolls back prepared transactions after `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`
Restart the database, which clears prepared transactions
Commit it: recovery reads the COMMIT line and runs `COMMIT PREPARED 'txf-5@payouts'` in the payouts database
quiz.why: The decision was made and written, and one side already committed, so the only outcome that keeps the payment whole is commit. Rolling it back would leave half a payment, the classic wrong guess made by hand. Prepared transactions survive restarts and have no timeout; they wait for someone to finish them.

quiz.q: A MongoDB transaction read `A-1001`'s balance, decided to debit it, and its update failed with `WriteConflict` labelled `TransientTransactionError`. What should the code do?
options: Retry only the failed update in the same session
Cancel, then run the whole transaction again, reads and decision included, on a new snapshot
Wait for the other transaction to commit, then carry on
Give up: write conflicts are permanent
quiz.why: Another transaction changed the document after this one's snapshot, so the balance it read is out of date, and the decision must be made again. MongoDB doesn't make one transaction's write wait for another's; the first writer wins. `withTransaction` in the Java driver runs this loop for you.

quiz.q: Which way of keeping transactions apart makes a long report block every writer of the rows it has read?
options: Serializable snapshot isolation
Snapshot isolation, where the first writer of a row wins
Strict two-phase locking: the report holds a shared lock on each row it read until it commits
Two-phase commit
quiz.why: Under strict two-phase locking, reads take shared locks held until commit, and a writer needs an exclusive lock, so it waits for the report. SSI and snapshot isolation let readers and writers pass each other. Two-phase commit is about committing on several machines, not about keeping transactions apart.

quiz.q: A payment debits a wallet kept in one program's PostgreSQL and credits a shop kept in another program's DynamoDB table. Which design fits?
options: One XA transaction across PostgreSQL and DynamoDB
A saga run by a workflow engine: a local debit recorded as pending, a credit keyed by the payment id so it can't happen twice, and a compensating refund if the credit can never succeed
A DynamoDB transaction that includes the PostgreSQL row
Commit PostgreSQL first, then DynamoDB, and raise an alert if the second fails
quiz.why: DynamoDB doesn't take part in XA, and its transactions cover only DynamoDB items, so no shared atomic commit exists here. A saga commits each step locally, makes each one safe to repeat, and repairs a failure that won't go away with a compensation, at the price of a visible pending state. Committing one side, then the other, is lesson 7's first version, which loses money whenever the second side fails.
